briefs.headline: CWC chief flags ‘malpractices’ in phytosanitary certification, pitches integrated logistics to boost agri-exports
briefs.deck: Santosh Sinha says CWC’s technical expertise and end-to-end logistics capabilities could help reduce export rejections
briefs.bodyText:
Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) Managing Director Santosh Sinha on Friday (September 19, 2026) raised concerns over what he described as “malpractices” in phytosanitary certification at ports, while declining to provide specific examples or name the entities involved.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of “Stakeholder Consultation on Strengthening Agri Export Logistics Through Integrated Warehousing and Value-Added Services”, organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) jointly with Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) in Chennai, Mr. Sinha was asked about his reference to malpractices in certification.
He said there had been “a certain result which was not to our liking”, but did not elaborate on the incident or identify any port, agency or official.
Mr. Sinha had raised the issue while explaining CWC’s plans to expand its role beyond conventional warehousing into integrated logistics for agricultural exports. He cited the rejection of Indian rice at Chinese ports and the rejection of mango exports by Japan as examples of the challenges Indian exporters could face when consignments fail to meet requirements in destination markets.
Asked how CWC could address the issue, Mr. Sinha said: “We have the kind of technical expertise that we have available with us.”
He said CWC was also upgrading its technical expertise, pointing to its experience in preserving food commodities. CWC currently stores around 50–60 lakh tonnes of foodgrains and, according to Mr. Sinha, less than 0.5% is lost during storage.
Mr. Sinha said the issue of export rejection was closely linked to phytosanitary requirements.
“Most of it is getting rejected on phytosanitary certifications,” he said.
He said India would encounter more such challenges as exports increase under free trade agreements.
“This is actually the sign of a growing economy. Because you are now going in for your free trade agreements, you will start exporting, you will encounter challenges, you will have to meet them,” he said.
During his address, Mr. Sinha said CWC could add a layer of phytosanitary treatment and preservation to the export supply chain to help ensure that agricultural produce was not rejected at destination ports. Referring to the rejection of Indian consignments, he claimed, “CWC would not have got rejected.”
CWC is seeking to expand its role in agricultural logistics by bringing together storage, preservation, grading, sorting, treatment, cold storage and transportation, with connectivity to ports.
CWC has at least four warehouses lined up for construction in Tamil Nadu this year, Mr. Sinha said, including facilities on the Chennai Outer Ring Road around Korattur/Poonamallee, at Red Hills, and at Theni and Gangaikondan.
CWC is targeting capital expenditure of about ₹1,000 crore this year, similar to the previous year, Mr. Sinha said. Around ₹400 crore would be spent on warehouse development, including land acquisition and construction, while the company is also investing in rail logistics.
Parallelly, the corporation is planning its first hyperloop freight trial at its CFS Logistics Park at JNPT, Mumbai, with a ₹23-crore order placed with IIT Madras-incubated TuTr Hyperloop. The 650-metre pilot, funded by CWC, will test the movement of containers using a Linear Induction Motor-based system, with the corporation also exploring a possible future application between ports and nearby container freight stations.
Initially, CWC envisages using the system to move containers between the port and container freight stations, Mr. Sinha said.
CWC placed the order in March or April this year. A tentative timeline of about a year had been indicated for the trial, he said, while cautioning that the project was an R&D exercise.
“We are willing to give them more time. The more important thing is that the solution should come up,” he said.
CWC will fund the pilot from its own resources, he said.
It has held stakeholder consultations in Mumbai, Delhi and Chennai as part of its effort to develop an integrated logistics solution for agricultural exports. Mr. Sinha said the feedback from the consultations would be compiled into a document, following which the corporation would prepare an action plan.

briefs.headline: Demand for next generation SME workspaces on the rise as promoters enter valuations game
briefs.bodyText:
Demand for office space is rising from a segment of Small & Medium Enterprises (SMEs) which are now moving to high-quality real estate from industrial galas [shop floor office] and nondescript locations, considering the astronomical high valuations seen through listings in SME exchanges.
The purpose is to meet clients and investors at a smart address as well as to provide employees a better work environmental, developers and analysts said.
To cater to this trend, developers are designing office buildings that specifically meet the requirement of this segment which needs about 1,000 to 5,000 sq ft office space in key locations.
In Mumbai upcoming micro–Central Business Districts (CBDs) like Ghatkopar, Andheri, Kurla, Powai are being considered by SME’s for new age Grade A office spaces that provide accessibility, connectivity, parking space, natural environment, larger common areas and modern amenities alongside core office space.
Raahul Maroo, Founder & Managing Director Tatvm Corp which is into real estate said, “We are seeing a rapid change in SMEs. The demand from them for Grade A office space is more for working area that would also attract institutional interest and create significant value for their clients.”
“SMEs are demanding offices that reflect the quality and ambition of their businesses within their constrained budgets. Understanding their needs we have created niche product offering to cater to their demand,” he said.
He said a segment of boutique developers is building smaller commercial offices spaces to for the SMEs segment.
As of September 2026, 136 SME IPOs have been listed of which several SME IPOs had an issue size between ₹25 crore and ₹150 crore.
This indicates the liquidity with segment. Besides, Government support has enabled this segment to have bigger ambitions.
Bappaditya Basu, Managing Director, Anarock Commercial said, “We are certainly witnessing a clear move by smaller businesses and start-ups from ad hoc or low-grade office space to professionally managed and also impressively addressed workspaces.”
“Startups are the largest consumers of flexible office space, comprising 37.5% of all flex seats rented on a national level, outnumbering the combined flex space rented by corporates and MNCs. The average deal size has also more than doubled in terms of seats per office space,” he said.
“This is reflective of a conscious shift by smaller occupiers toward quality, investor-ready locations, rather than continuing with cost-driven ones,” he stated.
“This has led developers and flex operators to design spaces for this segment, and it is one of the reasons why India has overtaken several Asia-Pacific markets to become the region’s largest flexible office sector,” he added.

briefs.headline: Who’s watching what we eat? Inside India’s food adulteration problem
briefs.deck: As adulteration cases pile up, and the Indian consumer confronts a complex food chain, where risks are often invisible, who’s responsible for keeping milk and everyday foods safe?
briefs.bodyText:
When Bikaner-based graphic designer Laxmi Rajpurohit, 22, began noticing changes in the taste, smell and consistency of the milk her family was getting from a big, reputed brand, she suspected foul play and decided to take things in her hands. She had read about simple ways of testing milk at home to check for water, starch or detergent. For instance, an iodine test would reveal starch if the milk turns blue-black. She picked up the water test from the Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test, or DART, programme manual of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).
She put droplets of the milk on a sloping surface. “It flowed quickly,” she says, “like water instead of leaving a thick white trail.” She complained to the company’s customer care, who asked her for further information about the product. She hasn’t heard back ever since.
Rajpurohit can test a drop of milk at home but the test cannot tell her everything that happened before the packet of milk reached her. It can’t tell her if the milk contains an adulterant or is contaminated or if it might fail some food safety standard.
The FSSAI has initiated legal action against Nestlé India over non-compliances with regards to regulations for infant food products.
Enough is enough
Between shiny paraffin-wax-coated apples, calcium carbide (“masala”) ripened mangoes, saw dust in red chilli powder, boric acid powder in maida and rice, and synthetic milk (detergent, urea, caustic soda, refined oils, milk powders, carbonates/ bicarbonates, melamine, heavy metals, pesticide residues), fake/ analogue paneer, and spurious ghee (dairy cream with palm oil and vanaspati), the average Indian is sick, cautious, angry and fed up. Milk, in particular, is consumed daily by infants up to the elderly, making itsadulteration a widespread public health and consumer safety concern.
Bengaluru-based doctor and food writer Nandita Iyer (@saffrontrail on Instagram) recalls how once an ice cream arrived looking like “some separated liquid or oil”. From then on, she has become really cautious. She checks labels carefully, sticks only to brands she trusts, and rarely orders fromrestaurantsnow.
Luke Coutinho, a wellness and lifestyle coach, argues that adulterated foods can add chemical stress burden to the body, triggering diseases. While “genuine mistakes happen sometimes,” he says, adding, the problem is “when companies/ brands with a running history of false marketing claims, fancy packaging, small print, wrong/misleading labels, and wrong accuracy, believe they can get away with it.” His advice is simple: stop buying from repeat offenders, encouraging others to boycott them, and buy instead from ethical brands.
The Supreme Court is now pushing FSSAI to set a clear timeline for introducing front-of-pack warning labels on unhealthy foods, while also urging stronger nutrition education in schools so consumers can make informed food choices.
Fraud remains invisible
“A home test may indicate some things. It cannot establish that everything else is absent. Moreover, a food laboratory can establish what is present in the sample but not if it is an intentional adulteration,” says Nilesh Amritkar, managing director of Envirocare Labs, an FSSAI notified food testing laboratory in Mumbai and Goa.
Amritkar uses detergent to explain the problem. “Detergent accidentally left on dairy equipment because it was not properly rinsed would be contamination. But if detergent were deliberately added to manipulate the appearance of milk, the same substance would become part of an adulteration,” he says. Heavy metals, pesticide residues, antibiotics or aflatoxin may make food unsafe without necessarily being adulterants. A product can be substandard because it fails a prescribed composition or quality benchmark without there being deliberate fraud.
In 2024-25, food-safety authorities analysed 1,70,535 enforcement samples and found 34,388 non-conforming, roughly one in five of the samples tested. Of these, 7,945 were classified as unsafe and 22,516 as substandard, while the rest involved labelling defects, misleading claims or other violations. While the numbers are significant, they cannot be read as a survey of everything we Indians eat. These were enforcement samples, often collected because regulators had a reason to look.
By the time a litre of milk reaches Rajpurohit’s or any kitchen in India, it may have passed through a long chain, running from the dairy farmer to the village collection centre, chilling facility and tanker, and then to a processing plant, packaging unit, distributor and retailer. The consumer doesn’t see the chain.
Unless one buys fresh, directly from farms. Consumers can purchase a greater degree of traceability. But not all farms might reveal if any banned antibiotics, hormones, or steroids were administered to their cows/ buffaloes, for instance.
Finding the sweet spot
In Kolkata, Partha Nandy, 42, has spent much of his life around milk. His family has owned Girish Ch. Dey & Nakur Ch. Nandy, the sweetmeat shop known for its kada-pak and naram-pak sandesh, since 1844. Nandy is its fifth-generation co-owner. The shop has maintained relationships with vendors for decades. Milk with added water produces less chhena. Adding milk powder for cost benefit produces low-quality, grainy chhena. During festivals, when demand for milk rises, these variations can become more common, he says.
Nandy adds he can also recognise impurities that appear during the preparation of chhena. The shop has historically relied on experience and relationships with suppliers rather than laboratory testing for adulterants. If there is something wrong with the milk, the vendor is warned. The problem, however, is that not every consumer is making sweets with it.
FSSAI’s risk-based inspection and surveillance system dates back to at least 2022. In 2026, FSSAI’s Central Advisory Committee called for intensified risk-based inspections and sustained surveillance of high-risk commodities such as milk and milk products, edible oils, spices and honey.
Milk illustrates the difficulty particularly well. The world’s largest milk producer, accounting for nearly 25% of global output, India produced nearly 248 million tonnes in 2024-25. In that period, the FSSAI’s data shows: of 33,405 milk samples tested, 12,780 were non-conforming. This does not mean 40% of India’s milk is defective, just that regulators found a significant number of problems. The consumer has no equivalent way of investigating.
Paneer presents similar challenges. An August briefing from the Centre for Health Equity flagged dairy analogues being sold as paneer. While not inherently unsafe, passing these off as traditional paneer is misleading. In Maharashtra, 109 of 308 samples were non-compliant between April 2025 and March 2026. Consequently, the FSSAI’s West Region has mandated accurate labelling for cheese analogues.
What can consumers do? Udai Kumar Saxena, a food-safety accreditation assessor and FSSAI-listed expert in risk assessment and analysis, says: “Check the date. Check the ingredients. Check the FSSAI number.” But exercise caution. An FSSAI licence or registration “establishes that the food business has entered the regulatory framework and is required to comply with its conditions but doesn’t mean the regulator has laboratory-tested and certified the packet in your hand,” he says. The law places the larger responsibility on the business and the regulator.
What the lab tells us
The regulator and the laboratory have different roles, but the objective is the same: “safer food”.
Ashwin Bhadri, founder-CEO of Navi Mumbai-headquartered Equinox Labs, which tests food, water and air, recalls a large food-service business that came to his laboratory concerned about the dairy product supplied to its kitchens. Tests showed it didn’t meet the expected specifications and indicated manipulation.
Equinox Labs, which has been working with food manufacturers, QSR (quick service restaurant) chains and cloud kitchens, for the last 21 years across five cities, have, at times, asked food companies to remove or review claims such as “100% pure” or “100% natural” when unsubstantiated. The big change now, Bhadri observes, is that individual restaurants, clubs, cafeterias, hospitals, and schools are starting to reach out to them for auditing.
“The FSSAI and FDA don’t care about intent. They care about the final outcome. Today, there are millions of SKUs (unique code or number to identify/ track products) in the market. One brand itself will have 50-100 different SKUs. FSSAI can’t test every batch, the country doesn’t have the budget or bandwidth,” says Bhadri, “One good thing FSSAI is doing is self-approval. They tell food brands to get their products tested by a third party and upload the quality reports to their websites. There’s a FosCos (Food Safety Compliance System) website, where regulation mandates uploading quality reports every six months.”
The lesson for Bhadri is that testing needs to happen before the inspector, or the customer, discovers the failure. “A food company shouldn’t discover a problem because an inspector found it,” he says. “It should discover the problem through its own quality-control system.” Testing, he says, should work as an early-warning system rather than a compliance formality.
Price of awareness
Another sample revealed microbiological contamination, including Coliforms, Enterobacteriaceae, E. coli, yeast, and mould. For an individual consumer, a food test at Equinox can cost between ₹500 and ₹25,000. A milk adulteration test may cost ₹1,000. A microbial safety test costs ₹1,500-₹2,000. A comprehensive panel covering pesticides, heavy metals and other tests can run into tens of thousands of rupees.
Iyer says, Bengaluru’s elite circles “use an app called FirstClub, launched a year ago, which runs all its products through a bunch of tests and only then lists them. The products aren’t all that more expensive.” The mass-y food aggregator apps can do these things. Since “it’s a huge loss for brands to not be listed on quick commerce, it could be a driving factor” [for change].
“Why should any consumer have to pay a premium merely to obtain food that is safe?” asks consumer-rights advocate Bejon Kumar Misra. A better-off consumer can choose an organised supermarket, a familiar brand or a subscription-based direct farm-to-home service. She can switch products when she loses trust. She can even pay for a laboratory test. “Money can buy more choices, but it cannot buy complete food safety,” adds Misra. Bhadri points to a section of society that does not read labels, or recognise food fraud when taste or consistency changes, and doesn’t have the money or power to pursue a complaint. The inequality here is glaring.
Making the system work
But here’s the thing: “As an individual, you don’t need to do this. Your job is simple. Just complain to FSSAI,” says Bhadri, mentioning that the Maharashtra FDA recently launched an AI portal to speed up food safety complaints, “where you literally talk and it will write the complaint for you”. The more privileged Indians complain, the more it benefits all Indians.
In the last few months, Mumbaikars have been tagging the FDA on social media and checking before eating if restaurants and packaged foods have passed the ‘Tukaram Mundhe test’. Mundhe, who took over as Maharashtra FDA commissioner in May, has been busting profiteering food-fraud rackets, seizing adulterated and suspect milk/ dairy products, and suspending licences across the State. Mundhe’s tenure illustrates what active enforcement can achieve — and its limits.
Can a suspect packet of milk/ paneer be quickly traced to the farm/ factory that made it and packaged it, revealing the ingredients used? So that consumers like Rajpurohit aren’t compelled to test at home/ labs? That brings us to the question of accountability: who is responsible? The manufacturer, to ensure quality control. And the regulator, to inspect, test, penalise and enforce. While the laboratory can establish what is present in a sample, and the consumer can identify irregularities and complain, their job is only to notice and report, not inspect, test, investigate, prove or prosecute.
Bhadri doesn’t believe in “more raids” but credits Mundhe for removing the “chalta hai” attitude. He says, “Enforcement is necessary, but enforcement alone won’t fix the system.” The goal, as Bhadri puts it, should be to “make adulteration difficult to do, easy to detect, and costly to ignore”.
The writer is a Kolkata-based freelance journalist.

briefs.headline: Maharashtra discom MSEDCL adopts AI, ML module to detect power theft
briefs.bodyText:
Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd (MSEDCL) said it had cracked down on power thieves across the state by leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) ‘Super Intelligence’.
Combining state-wide physical inspections by 190 “flying squads” with AI-driven predictive analysis, MSEDCL said it had exposed 27,964 instances of power theft worth ₹66.28 crore in three months.
Criminal cases have been registered in 289 instances where offenders failed to pay the assessed electricity charges and compounding fees.
MSEDCL said it had adopted dedicated AI and Machine Learning (ML) module to predict electricity theft accurately. Consumers exhibiting suspicious consumption patterns are automatically flagged under a ‘high-risk’ category, providing field teams with precise target locations without requiring prior manual surveys.
Lokesh Chandra,(IAS) Chairman & Managing Director, MSEDCL in a statement said, “Our target is to reduce MSEDCL’s Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses to below 10 percent over the next three years.”
“Prioritising the recovery of outstanding dues, an aggressive campaign against power theft is underway. The newly developed AI module has greatly intensified our precision and enforcement capabilities against electricity theft across the state,” he stated.
To execute ground-level actions based on AI intelligence, MSEDCL has deployed over 190 specialized “flying squads” across the state.
During the three-months from June to August, 2026 joint operations by the O&M and Security & Enforcement divisions exposed power thefts across all major regions: Konkan Region (11,083 cases), Pune Region (5,849 cases), Nagpur Region (5,949 cases), and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar Region (5,083 cases), the company said.
Out of the total 27,964 cases detected, formal assessment bills amounting to ₹66.28 crore were issued for 24,508 verified theft cases.
So far, MSEDCL has recovered ₹29.85 crore from 10,810 settled cases. Strict legal action is being initiated against those failing to clear dues within the stipulated period, with 289 criminal cases already registered, it said.

briefs.headline: NTPC terminates ₹413 crore BESS contract as contractor fails to meet obligations, achieve progress
briefs.deck: NTPC added that it has encashed ₹91 crore from GRIL’s bank guarantees.
briefs.bodyText:
State-owned power producer NTPC Ltd informed that it has terminated the contracted awarded to GR Infraprojects Ltd (GRIL) for building the 400 Megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system (BESS) project at its Mouda Super Thermal Power Station (Maharashtra) citing the latter’s inability to meet their contractual obligations and achieve required project progress.
The project – with a contract value of ₹413.37 crore – was awarded in March this year and was scheduled to be completed within fifteen months.
The contract stands terminated with immediate effect.
Explaining the cause for terminating the contract, NTPC stated, “The project witnessed significant delay in critical activities. A contractual notice was issued to GRIL calling for immediate corrective action, but GRIL failed to undertake the required remedial measures.”
NTPC added that it has encashed approximately ₹91 crore from the bank guarantees.
The power producer added that it has re-initiated re-tendering of the project.
“NTPC is taking necessary measures on priority to facilitate the early re-award and timely implementation of the project,” it stated.

briefs.headline: UPI MDR: Can Rs 6,000 be split into three Rs 2,000 payments? No daily cap
briefs.deck: The NPCI framework and the FAQs issued with it do not stipulate that multiple payments relating to a single bill must be clubbed together. Such a restriction, if in place, could prevent businesses from breaking up larger payments into multiple transactions of Rs 2,000 or less.
briefs.bodyText:
From October 15, 2026, 
UPI
 payments above Rs 2,000 made to large merchants will attract a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.4%. However, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) reportedly does not currently plan to introduce a separate daily limit on repeated UPI payments made to the same merchant.
Such a restriction, if in place, could prevent businesses from breaking up larger payments into multiple transactions of Rs 2,000 or less.
No daily cap on UPI right now
Under the framework that will take effect from October 15, regular merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000 will attract a 0.4% merchant discount rate, with the charge capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 or more.
For example, a merchant receiving a single UPI payment of Rs 6,000 would incur an MDR of Rs 24.
However, according to an ET report, instead of making one payment, the merchant could ask the customer to make three separate payments of Rs 2,000 each. Since each transaction would fall within the free limit, the merchant could avoid the Rs 24 charge, industry executives told the financial daily.
The NPCI framework and the FAQs issued with it do not stipulate that multiple payments relating to a single bill must be clubbed together.
“If the customer is willing to pay the merchant three times and both sides agree, it is between them. There is not much that can be done at the transaction level,” one person directly involved with NPCI told the financial daily. They also did not expect such workarounds to become significant over time.
Zero MDR loophole
Another potential gap relates to the zero-MDR person-to-person-merchant (P2PM) category available to small merchants. Banks and payment service providers track the UPI collections of merchants in this category and shift them to the regular merchant category if their collections cross Rs 1 lakh a month for three consecutive months.
The FAQs do not clarify whether a merchant’s collections have to be aggregated across different bank accounts, QR codes or payment service providers.
Industry executives said merchants could potentially distribute their receipts across these channels to keep each one below the prescribed threshold. Detecting such arrangements effectively would require linking the different accounts and payment channels to the same business.
Another possible workaround would be to direct business payments to personal UPI IDs, since person-to-person transactions continue to remain free regardless of the amount.
However, doing so would effectively present commercial receipts as personal transfers rather than using a legitimate exemption. Banks or payment providers could subsequently reclassify the account.
Businesses could also gain from being incorrectly assigned to a merchant category that attracts a flat Rs 5 charge instead of the 0.4% rate.
Railways, telecom services, insurance, fuel and utilities are among the categories eligible for concessional charges. Merchant category codes are assigned when a business is onboarded, and deliberately providing an incorrect classification would therefore amount to a breach of the rules, industry executives said.
Genuine recurring UPI AutoPay transactions are exempt from the charges. However, executives said treating an ordinary sale as a recurring payment merely to claim the exemption would constitute misclassification.
People familiar with the matter said NPCI expects some merchants to explore these workarounds once the new framework comes into effect. However, it does not currently believe additional transaction-level limits are necessary. The payments body also does not expect merchants splitting bills to become widespread or continue as a significant practice over the longer term.
More than 95% of merchant-payment volumes will continue to remain free under the framework. At the same time, industry estimates show that transactions above Rs 2,000 represent around two-thirds of the total value of merchant payments. This means widespread attempts to avoid the charges could have a meaningful impact on the collections expected under the new system.
NPCI has said the MDR revenue will be used to support UPI infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service.

stories.headline: Windies squad for India tour: Campbell returns; Pooran earns maiden T20I call-up
stories.deck: West Indies have recalled John Campbell for their ODI series against India, while Kamil Pooran earned his maiden T20I call-up after an impressive recent run. Shimron Hetmyer returns for the T20Is, with Jason Holder rested. The eight-match India tour will help West Indies prepare for the 2027 World Cup and build a strong core ahead of the next T20 World Cup.
stories.bodyText:
West Indies have brought back experienced opener John Campbell for their upcoming ODI series against India, while Kamil Pooran has received his first T20I call-up. The Caribbean side will face India in three ODIs and five T20Is from September 27 to October 17, with the series spread across eight cities.
Campbell returns after missing the last two ODIs against New Zealand because of a hamstring injury. Captain Shai Hope will lead the 15-member ODI squad, which also includes young batter Jewel Andrew. Andrew replaces Ackeem Auguste, who is still recovering from surgery he underwent in August.
Shimron Hetmyer, who featured in West Indies' final two ODIs against New Zealand, has been left out of the ODI squad. However, he will return for the T20I series after being given additional time to recover following the Caribbean Premier League.
India series a chance to prepare for World Cup
The first two ODIs against India will bring the automatic qualification phase for the 2027 ICC Men's ODI World Cup to an end. West Indies, however, will have to play a qualification tournament early next year after failing to finish ahead of their closest rivals in the standings.
Head coach Daren Sammy believes the India series will give his team a valuable chance to test themselves against the world's top-ranked ODI and T20I side and prepare for the World Cup.
"Playing against the top team in the world presents us with a chance to fine tune and improve our performances as an ODI team which has seen quality performances across the cycle," Sammy said.
In the T20I squad, the biggest talking point is the inclusion of Kamil, who has earned his maiden call-up after an impressive recent run. The right-handed opener scored 273 runs in eight innings at a strike rate of 159.64 and an average of 39.
Quentin Sampson, who was part of West Indies' T20 World Cup squad earlier this year in India, has also been selected. Experienced all-rounder Jason Holder, meanwhile, has been rested.
West Indies ODI squad: Shai Hope (captain), Jewel Andrew, John Campbell, Keacy Carty, Roston Chase, Matthew Forde, Justin Greaves, Amir Jangoo, Alzarri Joseph, Shamar Joseph, Vitel Lawes, Gudakesh Motie, Keemo Paul, Sherfane Rutherford, Jayden Seales.
 West Indies look to build for next T20 World Cup
The T20I squad also features Hope, Roston Chase, Hetmyer, Akeal Hosein, Rovman Powell, Sherfane Rutherford, Romario Shepherd and Shamar Springer.
"We are looking to build on the momentum from our series win against Sri Lanka, with the long-term goal of developing a strong core of players ahead of the next T20 World Cup," Sammy said.
The West Indies squad will leave the Caribbean on September 21 and reach Thiruvananthapuram on September 23, four days before the ODI series begins.
West Indies T20I squad: Shai Hope (captain), Jewel Andrew, Roston Chase, Matthew Forde, Shimron Hetmyer, Akeal Hosein, Shamar Joseph, Gudakesh Motie, Keemo Paul, Kamil Pooran, Rovman Powell, Sherfane Rutherford, Quentin Sampson, Romario Shepherd, Shamar Springer.

stories.headline: Davis Cup: Czechs beat USA to qualify for finals
stories.deck: The wins in Davis Cup are always a little bit different because this is a team competition, said Jiri Lehecka
stories.bodyText:
Jiri Lehecka downed Learner Tien in a deciding rubber Saturday (September 19, 2026) as the Czech Republic stunned the United States 3-2 in Davis Cup qualifying for a second straight year, while South Korea reached the last eight for the first time.
The Czechs knocked out the Americans at the same second qualifying round stage in a decider at Delray Beach a year ago, when Jakub Mensik beat Frances Tiafoe to secure a surprise victory.
Tomas Berdych's men repeated the feat in similarly dramatic fashion, to the delight of a raucous home crowd in Prague, as Lehecka clinched a 6-3, 7-5 win over world number 13 Tien.
The U.S.A. are record 32-time winners of the competition but their wait for a first title since 2007 goes on.
The Czechs advance to the November eight-team finals in Bologna, where hosts Italy will bid for a fourth straight title.
"The wins in Davis Cup are always a little bit different because this is a team competition," said Lehecka.
After starting the day locked at 1-1, the USA nudged ahead as Christian Harrison and Austin Krajicek saved four match points to outlast Adam Pavlasek and Patrik Rikl in a thrilling 5-7, 6-3, 7-6 (10/8) win.
Mensik then fought back from a set down to keep the tie alive by defeating recent US Open runner-up Ben Shelton 5-7, 6-4, 6-3.
Shelton took a tense first set after saving a set point when trailing 5-4, reeling off the last three games.
Mensik created a set point at exactly the same stage of the second, but this time made no mistake with a booming forehand to level the match.
The 21-year-old, a semi-finalist at this year's French Open, forced the tie into a deciding rubber on his second match point in a tense final game.
Lehecka, who beat Shelton in straight sets on Friday (September 18, 2026), recovered after giving an early break back to take the first set.
Tien forged 3-0 ahead as he attempted to force the tie to a final set, but fell away and Lehecka clinched the win on his fourth match point.
"I must say it has been a great week. But, most importantly, we made it through as a team," Lehecka said. "Without Jakub winning against Ben, I would not have the chance to play the final match."
History-making South Korea
Earlier, South Korea made history by beating India 3-1 in Seoul.
Kwon Soon-woo brushed aside Sumit Nagal 6-1, 6-2 to clinch the decisive point for the Koreans, who won both Friday's singles rubbers before India triumphed in the doubles.
"I feel very proud for my country and every team I play against, I give my best," said Kwon.
Canada beat France 3-1 at Quebec City to reach the last eight.
Benjamin Bonzi and Pierre-Hugues Herbert beat Felix Auger-Aliassime and Duncan Chan 7-6 (7/4), 6-3 in doubles to keep France in the fight after two singles losses on Friday.
World number five Auger-Aliassime would not be denied, however, as he rallied to defeat France's Arthur Rinderknech 4-6, 7-6 (7/5), 6-4 to ensure Canada advanced.
The Canadians last won the Davis Cup in 2022 while France has not hoisted the trophy since 2017.
Austria booked their spot as Jurij Rodionov sealed a 3-1 win for the hosts in Vienna with a 7-6 (8/6), 6-3 victory over Zizou Bergs, Belgium's number one in the absence of Alexander Blockx.
Newly crowned U.S. Open champion Alexander Zverev gave Germany a 1-0 lead over Croatia in Halle, making a quick return to action as he beat Matej Dodig 6-4, 7-6 (7/3).
But Germany, who have not won the Davis Cup since 1993, were pegged back to end the first day level as Croatian youngster Dino Prizmic brushed aside Daniel Altmaier 6-4, 6-3.
Spain continued their tilt at a seventh title by seizing a 2-0 lead over Chile in Santiago courtesy of singles wins for Daniel Merida and Davis Cup debutant Rafael Jodar over Alejandro Tabilo and Cristian Garin, respectively.
Britain's Toby Samuel overcame Andres Andrade of Ecuador and Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery saw off Alvaro Guillen Meza as the hosts took a 2-0 advantage in London.

stories.headline: Raphinha hat-trick maintains Barcelona’s perfect LaLiga start
stories.deck: Barcelona moved provisionally six points clear of second-placed Real Madrid, ‌who have a game in hand and play Atletico Madrid on September 20, 2026
stories.bodyText:
Barcelona maintained their perfect start to the LaLiga season with a 3-1 victory at Sevilla on Saturday (September 19, 2026) as captain Raphinha scored a hat-trick to continue his prolific opening to the campaign.
Youssouf Fofana headed Sevilla in front after 18 minutes, but Raphinha equalised four minutes later before adding two second-half goals to seal Barcelona's seventh successive league win.
Barcelona moved provisionally six points clear of second-placed Real Madrid, who have a game in hand and play Atletico Madrid on Sunday (September 20, 2026).
Sevilla matched the visitors in a tentative start in which goalkeeper Odysseas Vlachodimos produced a brilliant save to deny Lamine Yamal.
The hosts then became only the second team to take the lead against Barcelona this season when Felix Correia clipped in a cross from the left and Fofana headed past Dominik Livakovic, who was deputising for the injured Joan Garcia.
Barcelona responded quickly as Raphinha ran on to Andreas Christensen's pass and calmly beat Vlachodimos.
Sevilla continued to make life uncomfortable for Barcelona, who were struggling to create chances, and almost retook the lead before halftime. An inspired Fofana backheel released Correia, but Rodri made a goal-saving tackle.
Raphinha headed in his second goal in the 52nd minute following good footwork from Lamine in the box, and the Brazilian was inches away from a third when his corner hit the post.
He did complete his hat-trick in the 69th minute, racing behind the Sevilla defence to convert another Lamine assist for his 12th league goal in seven matches.
Barcelona controlled possession as the game fizzled out in the closing stages and threatened to add a fourth as Sevilla's challenge faded, although Christensen's second-half injury was a concern for Hansi Flick.
The Barca coach will have been encouraged by the way his side reacted with poise after falling behind and by their ability to find a way through once Sevilla's pressing had frustrated them in the first half.
Earlier on Saturday (September 19), Osasuna drew 1-1 with Rayo Vallecano, while Athletic Club and Alaves played out a goalless draw. Celta Vigo secured their first triumph of the season in emphatic fashion with a 5-0 win over Racing Santander.

stories.headline: Asian Games: Quimcy Dsouza falls short in bronze battle
stories.bodyText:
Quimcy Dsouza had a 10-7 lead against world No. 7 Sakamoto Yuina, but the Japanese player is drawing on her experience to turn the bronze-medal match around.
Sakamoto’s deft touches and varied range of shots have put Quimcy under increasing pressure, with the Japanese player clawing her way back to 10-all.
And now, heartbreakingly for India, Sakamoto has earned match point.
Quimcy Dsouza refused to go down without a fight. After the timeout, the Indian saved the set point and levelled the score at 11-all against Sakamoto Yuina.
But despite pushing the world No. 7 all the way, Quimcy could not clear the final hurdle. Sakamoto held her nerve to seal the victory and claim the bronze medal.
It may not have been the finish Quimcy wanted, but this has been a memorable run, and hopefully the first of many more big moments on the international stage.
India’s Sonam Uttam Maskar has surged into second place in the women’s 10m air rifle qualification after registering a score of 349.8 at the end of Series 4.
Vidarsa K. Vinod is also currently inside the qualification cut, sitting eighth with 305.1 after Series 3. Only the top eight shooters will advance to the final.
What a fightback from Quimcy Dsouza, but the Indian was left frustrated at the finish. Trailing 7-9 against Japan’s Sakamoto Yuina, she won four of the next five points to move 11-10 ahead.
Sakamoto, however, held her nerve to level the score at 11-all before taking the next two points. Quimcy has now lost the opening set and trails 0-1 in the bronze-medal match.
Quimcy Dsouza has made a fast start in the women’s singles bronze-medal match, racing into a 4-1 lead against Japan’s Sakamoto Yuina.
A quick reminder of the format: the first player to reach 12 points takes the set, with the bronze-medal contest being played as a best-of-three.
India’s wait for its first medal at the Asian Games could end soon, with Quimcy Dsouza taking centre stage in the women’s singles bronze-medal match.
The Maharashtra player, who had fans across the country brushing up on Teqball rules on Saturday, is up against Japan’s Sakamoto Yuina in the medal clash.
Quimcy will be hoping to cap her impressive campaign with a bronze and get India on the medal table.
India’s Suraj Singh Mayanglambam posted a score of 9.683 in the men’s Changquan final at the Asian Games.
He earned a perfect 5.000 in the A Group for Quality of Movement and a full 2.000 in the C Group for Degree of Difficulty. His B Group score for Overall Performance was 2.683.
The combined score places Suraj Singh 10th in the standings at this stage.
The women’s 10m air rifle individual qualification is set to begin shortly, with three Indian shooters in the 60-member field.
Elavenil Valarivan, Sonam Uttam Maskar and Vidarsa K. Vinod will be aiming to finish inside the top eight to secure a place in the final. With only eight spots available from the 60-shooter qualification round.
India’s first event of the day at the Asian Games in Japan is underway, with Suraj Singh Mayanglambam competing in the men’s Changquan final in wushu.
The event features 20 participants, with the competitors being assessed on a 10-point scale across three categories. Quality of Movement, or Group A, carries a maximum of five points, while Overall Performance in Group B is worth three points. The remaining two points are awarded for Degree of Difficulty, known as Group C or Nandu.
Changquan, meaning ‘Long Fist’, is a traditional form of wushu that originated in northern China. It is known for its extended kicks, striking movements and acrobatic elements, with the modern discipline placing a strong emphasis on flexibility, athleticism and precision.
India have previously won 10 Asian Games medals in wushu, including two silver and eight bronze. Suraj Singh will now look to add to that tally as the Changquan final gets underway.

briefs.headline: Martin recovers from early setback to win Austrian sprint and retake championship lead
briefs.deck: ‘I am really happy for my team because they really deserve it; we are ready for tomorrow; I hope that we can continue at this pace,’ said Jorge Martin
briefs.bodyText:
Aprilia's Jorge Martin made an extraordinary recovery from a chaotic opening-lap battle with championship rival Marc Marquez to win the Austrian Grand Prix sprint from pole position on Saturday (September 19, 2026) and reclaim the MotoGP championship lead.
Martin, who had stormed to pole position ahead of reigning MotoGP champion Marquez earlier on Saturday (September 18), beat the Ducati rider to claim his 20th sprint victory after KTM's Pedro Acosta crashed out while leading in the closing stages.
The 28-year-old Martin, the 2024 MotoGP champion, now has 286 points in the standings, three ahead of Spanish compatriot Marquez, heading into Sunday's Grand Prix at the Red Bull Ring in Spielberg.
Martin's race appeared to unravel in the opening corners when he was forced on to the defensive by seven-time MotoGP champion Marquez, ran wide and dropped to eighth.
Acosta capitalised to take command and built a lead of nearly three seconds, only to crash out with about three laps remaining at KTM's home circuit.
Martin, meanwhile, carved his way back through the pack to secure a remarkable victory.
"I enjoyed the race for sure," Martin said. "I was a bit lucky with Pedro because we thought that I would be second. We started well but then we were on the limit on the first lap, so I thought my chances were over.
"But then, lap by lap, I didn't give up during the race. I was pushing till my maximum, trying to be super concentrated to come from the back and then win. The end was so good.
"I am really happy for my team because they really deserve it. We are ready for tomorrow. I hope that we can continue at this pace."
Marquez had seized the championship lead for the first time this season by winning last weekend's chaotic San Marino Grand Prix. The result had left him level on points with Martin but the 33-year-old moved to the top of the standings by virtue of having won more races this season.
"Today the target was third place in the sprint and I tried not to lose a lot of points against Jorge because it's already in practice that Pedro and Jorge had a better pace," Marquez said.
"Then I found the position where I sat just behind Jorge, and we were a bit lucky with Pedro's mistake. But happy and ready for tomorrow."
Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi, third in the championship standings, completed the podium.
Trackhouse Aprilia's Ai Ogura finished fourth with Alex Marquez fifth.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: One Asia, one heart as continental extravaganza begins
briefs.deck: Emperor Naruhito formally declares the mega event open; host Japan’s entry during the parade of nations expectedly draws the loudest cheers
briefs.bodyText:
Games with a Heart. The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games opening ceremony left no one in doubt on what the city and the organisers were aiming at at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya on Saturday (September 19, 2026), the heart, in all its myriad symbolism pervading every aspect of the event.
Throughout the approximately 110-minute presentation, the repeated emphasis on heart, unity and oneness was unmissable, right from the heart-shaped, inclined stage in the middle of the field to the placards carrying the teams’ names during the athletes parade. Even the outfits for performers accompanying violinist and composer Taro Hakase during his recital were heart-shaped, as were the ‘angel drones’ dressed up in flowing fabric, invoking the diversity and solidarity of Asian countries.
“This giant heart, being born from a fusion of diverse artists, performers, visuals, stage mechanisms, and systems, is sure to become a message originating in Aichi-Nagoya that spreads to Asia and even to the entire world. People around the globe will relate to and connect with each other through joy and friendship,” chief creative director Yukihiko Tsutsumi said in a statement.
He didn’t need to spell it out. Everything in front of the packed stands of the completely rebuilt, rechristened 35,000 capacity Paloma Mizuho Stadium that was formally opened only in April made it amply clear that the city was keen on showcasing itself as a centre for hospitality, culture and performing arts, the opening ceremony’s design concept itself titled ‘Harmonic Heart Beat’. Even the cauldron that was lit at the end of the ceremony was heart-shaped to depict one Asia, one heart, hammer throw legend Shigenobu Murofushi, accompanied by his Olympic champion son Koji Murofushi, doing the honours.
Host Japan’s entry during the parade of nations expectedly drew the loudest cheers, matched only by the welcome for the royal family, with Emperor Naruhito formally declaring the Games open. Earlier, the pre-show that started at 4 p.m. included performances by artists from the Shigo Bonote Preservation Society and the INI Music Group.
With the Nagoya Castle at its centre, the ‘Heart Beat of Tradition’ had performances by kabuki artists before the past made way to the present and future, the inevitability of Aichi-Nagoya’s industrial might too big to be ignored even in the midst of all the heart on display. But even there, the display made references to the historical origins of the city’s manufacturing prowess.
The extent of technology integration with everyday life meant many of the songs used during the ceremony were created with AI. But the messaging was plain — beyond the heavy industry that it is known for and the mechanical excellence it prides on, Nagoya’s ambitions were now bigger, embracing its historical past as well as its softer side to attract more people than just the hard-nosed businessmen.

briefs.headline: Arsenal thrashed by Brighton, sorry Spurs lose again
briefs.deck: Brighton deserved to win the game. We didn't do the basics right for long periods, said Arsenal coach Mikel Arteta
briefs.bodyText:
Arsenal's perfect start to their Premier League title defence came off the rails in a 3-0 trouncing by Brighton on Saturday (September 20, 2026), while Tottenham remain winless after a 3-2 defeat to Aston Villa.
Mikel Arteta's men arrived on the south coast in formidable form having won all seven games in all competitions this season.
But it was Brighton's fine start to the campaign that was maintained as goals from Pascal Gross, Charalampos Kostoulas and Chema Andres breached the Gunners' normally impenetrable defence.
"Brighton deserved to win the game. We didn't do the basics right for long periods," said Arteta.
"It's a big lesson for us to learn. How the team has played and competed in the last six or seven weeks has been expectational, but today has been a big lesson."
It is the third consecutive season that the Premier League champions have lost at the Amex after Liverpool and Manchester City in the past two years.
Brighton were full of confidence after becoming the first side in 50 years to come from 2-0 down to beat Manchester United at Old Trafford in the League Cup in midweek.
Fabian Hurzeler's side went at Arsenal from the start but had to wait until 31 minutes for the opener when Gross crashed a shot in off the inside of the post.
Arsenal were punished for allowing too much space on the edge of their area again just before half-time when Kostoulas this time picked his spot to beat David Raya.
Rather than a rousing second-half response, the visitors fell further behind on the hour mark as Andres was afforded the space to head in Gross's corner inside the six-yard box for Brighton's 16th goal in five league games this season.
"It was a special win. Not only because we played the best team in England but because of the performance," said Hurzeler. "I am really proud of my team."
The defeat is Arsenal's heaviest in any competition since April 2023.
Spurs ‘too fragile’
It was also another day to forget for Arsenal's north London rivals as Tottenham will have to stew over a three-week international break in the relegation zone.
After four games without a goal, an end to Spurs' drought came too late as they were already 3-0 down before two consolation strikes from Conor Gallagher and Jan Paul van Hecke.
Villa were indebted to goalkeeper Zion Suzuki for a string of saves to keep them in the game before Johan Manzambi slotted the visitors ahead at the end of the first half.
Nicolas Jackson exposed some woeful Spurs defending to add a second before a brilliant strike from Emi Buendia secured Villa's first league win of the season.
"We played well in the first half, we didn't score, but [we are] too fragile," said Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi.
"The moment when we have to defend, we have to defend compact. The leaders have to be leaders and to lead the team."
Tottenham could even go into the international break bottom if Fulham avoid defeat against Manchester United on Sunday (September 20, 2026), after Coventry broke their duck with a 1-0 win over Nottingham Forest.
Jay Dasilva scored the only goal to give the Sky Blues their first Premier League win for 25 years.

Konstantinos Tzolakis saved Yoane Wissa's penalty before half-time to keep Hull alive, and they produced a nervy finish at St. James' Park when Mohamed-Ali Cho pulled a goal back.

briefs.headline: England sweep Sri Lanka 3-0, replace India at top of T20I rankings
briefs.deck: England beat Sri Lanka by eight wickets in the third T20I at Old Trafford in Manchester on Saturday to complete a 3-0 series sweep. The hosts chased down Sri Lanka's 125-run target with 62 balls to spare. The win also helped England move back to the top of the T20 world rankings, replacing India.
briefs.bodyText:
England beat Sri Lanka by eight wickets in the third T20I at Old Trafford in Manchester on Saturday to complete a 3-0 series sweep.
The hosts chased down Sri Lanka's 125-run target with 62 balls to spare. The win also helped England move back to the top of the T20 world rankings, replacing India.
It was England's 15th straight T20 win over Sri Lanka.
Buttler leads easy chase
Sri Lanka were bowled out for 124 with seven balls left in their innings.
Pathum Nissanka top-scored with 36 off 24 balls, while Kamindu Mendis made 35 off 28. Will Jacks, Jofra Archer and Player of the Match Sonny Baker took two wickets each for England.
England lost opener Aneurin Donald for 13, but 
Jos Buttler
 and 
Harry Brook
 quickly took control.
Buttler smashed an unbeaten 62 off 32 balls, while Brook made 33. England reached 126-2 in just 9.4 overs.
Buttler had earlier become the first batter to score 15,000 career T20 runs on Thursday.
Brook, Asalanka reflect on series
Brook finished as the highest run-scorer and was named Player of the Series.
"I think everybody stepped up in this series," said Brook. "Every game has been slightly different and we're playing the conditions extremely well."
Sri Lanka's bowling also struggled, giving away nine wides, including two that went for four.
Sri Lanka captain Charith Asalanka called the series a major disappointment for his team.
"A very disappointing series for us in both the major departments, batting and bowling... this is an important eye-opener for us of where we stand right now in T20 cricket comparing to the best teams in the world," said Asalanka.
"This is a time to get together as players, support staff, and our Sri Lanka cricket board as well to find solutions for these T20 problems. These are the best 15 players right now so we have to find solutions in the right way."
England had won the first T20I in Southampton by 119 runs, with Brook scoring an unbeaten 114.
England will next face Sri Lanka in three ODIs, starting at Durham's Chester-le-Street on Tuesday.

briefs.headline: Father-son duo makes history: Shigenobu and Koji light cauldron
briefs.deck: Japan’s Shigenobu Murofushi and his son Koji Murofushi jointly lit the cauldron at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, bringing the torch relay to a memorable end. Both Shigenobu and Koji are former Asian Games champions in hammer throw. The duo climbed the stairs to the podium together before lighting the cauldron.
briefs.bodyText:
A father and son who built their legacy in hammer throw shared one of the biggest moments of the 
Asian Games
 opening ceremony on Saturday.
Japan’s Shigenobu Murofushi and his son Koji Murofushi jointly lit the cauldron at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, bringing the torch relay to a memorable end.
Both Shigenobu and Koji are former Asian Games champions in hammer throw. The duo climbed the stairs to the podium together before lighting the cauldron.
The ceremony featured dance, music and fireworks as the Asian Games officially opened in Aichi-Nagoya.
From Olympic champion to father-son moment
The cauldron lighting was the final part of a relay involving some of Japan’s biggest sporting names.
Women’s wrestler Fujinami Akari brought the torch into the stadium before passing it to four-time Olympic swimming champion Kitajima Kosuke.
The torch then went to Ito Koji, a three-time gold medallist in athletics at the 1998 Bangkok Asian Games. Takahashi Ayaka, the 2016 Rio Olympics badminton women’s doubles champion, was next.
Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi (Reuters Photo)
The torch was then handed to Koji Murofushi, the 2004 Athens Olympics hammer throw champion.
The final torchbearer was his father, Shigenobu Murofushi, who won the Asian Games hammer throw title five times in a row.
The two then came together to light the cauldron, which had a metallic design inspired by the shape of a heart.
Who is Shigenobu Murofushi?
Shigenobu Murofushi is one of Japan’s most successful hammer throwers. He competed at three Olympic Games — Munich 1972, Montreal 1976 and Los Angeles 1984.
He also served as Japan’s flag-bearer at the 1984 Olympics.
Murofushi initially tried sumo and shot put before taking up hammer throw. In 1984, he set a Japanese record of 75.96m. That mark remained the national record until his son Koji broke it in 1998.
Shigenobu won the Asian Games hammer throw gold medal in 1970, 1974, 1978, 1982 and 1986. He also won silver in 1966.
His Asian Games medal record includes five gold medals and one silver.
He also won gold at the 1979 and 1981 Asian Championships.
Shigenobu’s Olympic journey
While Shigenobu dominated the Asian Games, an Olympic medal remained out of reach.
He finished eighth at the 1972 Munich Olympics, 11th at Montreal 1976 and 15th at Los Angeles 1984.
His son would later achieve what he could not at the Olympics.
Koji Murofushi followed his father’s footsteps
Koji started hammer throw at the age of 10 under the guidance of his father.
He went on to become one of the leading hammer throwers in the world. Koji won the silver medal at the 2001 World Championships before claiming bronze in 2003.
His biggest Olympic moment came at the 2004 Athens Games, where he won the hammer throw gold medal.
He added an Olympic bronze at the 2012 London Games.
Koji also became world champion in 2011 in Daegu.
Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi (Reuters Photo)
Koji’s Asian Games medal record
Koji continued his family’s success at the Asian Games.
He won gold in hammer throw at Bangkok in 1998 and Busan in 2002. He had earlier won silver at Hiroshima in 1994.
His Asian Games record therefore includes two gold medals and one silver.
Koji also won gold at the 2002 Asian Championships and three silver medals at the continental championships in 1993, 1995 and 1998.
A family legacy comes full circle
The Murofushis have now added another special chapter to their long sporting legacy.
Shigenobu dominated the Asian Games in the 1970s and 1980s. Koji followed him into the event and later became an Olympic and world champion.
On Saturday, the father and son stood together at the centre of the Asian Games opening ceremony — not to compete, but to light the flame that officially began the Games.
Glittering opening ceremony
The 20th Asian Games officially began in Nagoya with a two-hour opening ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. Japan's Emperor Naruhito officially declared the Games open. Empress Masako, members of the Japanese imperial family, Olympic Council of Asia president Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani and International Olympic Committee president Kirsty Coventry were also present at the ceremony.
The event started with the Japanese national anthem and the raising of the national flag. Nine members of the Japanese Self-Defence Forces carried the flag to the stage before it was hoisted.
The stadium was then turned dark, with a spotlight focused on the Japanese flag.
The ceremony was followed by the parade of athletes. Teams from 45 nations and regions took part, along with the OCA Refugee Team, taking the total number of participating delegations to 46.

briefs.headline: Tom Brady’s 2019 Patriots jersey sells for $273,107 after photo match
briefs.deck: At auction, Tom Brady's 2019 New England Patriots jersey sold for an astonishing $273,107, marking a significant moment when he overtook Peyton Manning on the all-time passing yards leaderboard. The auction attracted intense competition with twenty-four bids, driven by the item's authentication and photo-matching details, demonstrating the high value placed on memorabilia from Brady's illustrious…
briefs.bodyText:
Tom Brady’s game-worn New England Patriots jersey from a memorable 2019 game against the New York Giants has now sold for $273,107 at auction. Brady wore the jersey on a night when he passed Peyton Manning to move into second place on the NFL’s all-time passing yards list. The jersey was sold through Grey Flannel Auctions after attracting 24 bids.
Tom Brady jersey from historic Patriots win draws major interest
The jersey came from New England’s 35-14 win over the Giants on October 10, 2019. Brady had a strong night, completing 31 passes for 334 yards while also scoring two rushing touchdowns. The game became even more important because his passing total pushed him past Manning on the NFL’s career list.
Grey Flannel Auctions listed the jersey with an opening bid of $25,000. During the auction, interest continued to grow, with the highest reported bid reaching $203,507 before the auction closed. The auction house later listed the final sale at $273,107, with 24 bids recorded.
The jersey was part of Grey Flannel’s August 16, 2026 Photo-Matched Auction. The auction ran from July 24 through August 16, with the prices shown by the auction house including the buyer’s premium.
Why the 2019 game made Brady’s jersey special
Brady’s performance against the Giants was not just another regular-season game. 
Passing Manning on the career passing yards list gave the jersey a direct connection to an important point in Brady’s career.
The item also came with authentication and photo-matching documentation. According to the auction listing, the jersey had an NFL certificate of authenticity and a MeiGray photo match. The MeiGray documentation noted identifying details on the jersey, helping connect the actual piece of clothing to Brady’s use during the game.
That kind of documentation matters in the sports memorabilia market. A jersey can become much more valuable when collectors can connect it to one specific game or achievement rather than simply showing that it belonged to a famous player.
Brady’s memorabilia has already reached much higher prices. His final NFL game-worn Tampa Bay Buccaneers jersey sold for $1.391 million through RM Sotheby’s in 2023. The jersey was worn during his final game against the Dallas Cowboys and was photo-matched to the third and fourth quarters.
In 2026, Joe Montana’s Super Bowl XXIV jersey also set a new reported NFL jersey record at $1.515 million, according to Goldin. That sale moved past Brady’s 2023 result.
Still, the $273,107 price for Brady’s 2019 Patriots jersey shows how much collectors value items tied to specific moments from his career. This was not simply a jersey worn during a Patriots win. It was the jersey Brady wore when he moved past Manning on the NFL’s passing yards list, giving the piece a clear place in football history.
